summary: They had no network in Denmark and got few replies at first. Their public data projects became the main topic in their interviews.
similarities: Like many international graduates, they started their job search in Denmark without a professional network.
They applied in English and did not speak Danish when they were hired.
differences: They have a technical MSc in Data Science from DTU, which may differ from your education.
They found the job through the company career page, not through a referral.
lessons: Build one or two small projects on data that Danish employers care about, and link them at the top of your CV.
Replace generic applications with examples of real work you can talk about in an interview.

summary: They were turned down by Danish-language finance roles and changed focus to English-speaking teams. Their student job gave them their strongest reference.
similarities: They studied in Denmark and had limited Danish (A2) during their job search.
They faced job ads that asked for fluent Danish.
differences: Their background is in finance and accounting, which may not be your field.
They had 18 months of relevant student job experience before applying.
lessons: Target companies with English-speaking teams instead of sending many applications to Danish-language roles.
Treat your student job as real experience and ask your manager to be a reference.

summary: They changed career from mechanical engineering to a business analyst role. A LinkedIn post and informal coffee meetings led to a referral.
similarities: They had to explain how earlier experience fits a new kind of role, which many job seekers find hard.
They had only basic Danish (A1) when they were hired.
differences: They had three years of work experience as an engineer before their master's.
They were hired through a referral, which depends on the network you build.
lessons: Connect your past experience to the role you want in one clear sentence.
Ask a few people in your target field for short, informal coffee meetings.
